newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour leader Blair to push education.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour leader Blair to push education.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party will couple a withering attack on Prime Minister John Major on Saturday with a renewed promise to make education the main plank of its campaign at the forthcoming general election.

Aides of Labour leader Tony Blair said he intended to underscore his commitment to raise Britain's school standards by promising to plough into education money saved by getting people off welfare, thus "reducing the cost of failure".
Blair is due to give the keynote speech at the party's local government conference in Nottingham, central England, on Saturday (Eds: 1145 GMT).
It could be Blair's last set-piece speech at a national conference before the election, which must take place by May 22 but might come as early as next month.

Blair, whose party holds a 15-20 percent lead in opinion polls, believes education will be the number one issue at the election and aides, who trailed his speech in advance, say he is determined to force the pace.
With voter surveys showing Major more popular than the Conservative Party he heads, Blair is expected to mount a personal attack on the prime minister as a weak leader.

He will portray him as paralysed by factional in-fighting in the Conservative Party and argue that Britain's isolation in Europe, the crisis over mad cow disease and higher taxes are illustrations of "failure and betrayal" that can be traced back to weak leadership.
"In an uncertain world, Britain cannot afford an uncertain leader," Blair, whose party has been in opposition since 1979, is expected to say.

The promise to increase the proportion of national income spent on education is the first chapter of a 10-part "contract with the people" that will form the basis of Labour's election manifesto, officials said.

Blair set out the contract at Labour's annual conference last October. It also includes promises to halve the number of youth unemployed, to keep borrowing and inflation low and to devolve power from London to Scotland and Wales.

Staking so much on education is not a risk-free strategy for Labour. The party's education spokesman, David Blunkett, was engulfed in controversy on Friday after he backed away in a newspaper interview from ambitions to abolish grammar schools that select their pupils according to ability.
"This is just another example of Labour trying to catch up with our agenda, having opposed it every step of the way," Education Secretary Gillian Shephard said.
But Blair's aides said he would praise Blunkett on Saturday as one of Labour's real stars.
He would also encourage Blunkett to keep up pressure on the Conservatives with fresh initiatives aimed at raising school standards, improving pupil discipline and involving parents.
